title: Terraform basics

story: The sandbox VMs come in sizes. Each size is described by a launch template, a saved recipe in AWS that says which machine type, which image and which disk a new VM gets. Today there are two sizes, lite and full, and your task is to add a third one, wide, for the big tickets.

You could click through the AWS console, but then nobody can review your change, and nobody can rebuild it if it disappears. You could write a script that creates three launch templates, but the second time it runs it tries to create lite and full again, and if someone deleted full by hand last week, it does something nobody planned. What you really want is to write the three sizes down once, and have a tool tell you, before it touches anything, exactly what it is about to create, change or destroy.
hook.question: How does a tool know what already exists, and how can I see what it will change before it changes anything?

p: Terraform reads files that describe the infrastructure you want, and makes the real world match them. The files are written in HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language), a small language of blocks with name = value lines inside. Our infrastructure repo uses OpenTofu, an open-source fork of Terraform: the language and the commands are the same, only the program is called tofu instead of terraform. Everything in this lesson works with either one.

The new part is the way you think. A script is a list of actions: create this, then create that. A Terraform file describes the result: there should be one launch template per size. This style is called declarative, and you already know it from React. You describe what the screen should look like, and React calculates which DOM changes get it there. Terraform calculates the changes for your infrastructure in the same way, and the list of changes it calculates is called the plan. The comparison stops at memory, though. React keeps its last picture in memory and can always compare against it, while Terraform needs a file to remember what it created last week. That file is the subject of the next section.

Two more words before the code. A provider is a plugin that knows how to talk to one system: the aws provider calls the AWS API, and the local provider, which we use in the lab, writes files on your disk. A resource is one thing that a provider manages, such as one launch template or one file. Every resource has an address made of its type and its name, like local_file.template, and Terraform uses that address everywhere: in plans, in errors and in its memory.

notes.text: Which provider, from which registry, at an exact version. tofu init downloads it and records its checksum in .terraform.lock.hcl, which you commit, like package-lock.json.
A variable is an input with a type, much like a function parameter with a default value.
resource "<type>" "<name>": the address of this block is local_file.template.
for_each makes one resource per entry of the map. Their addresses are local_file.template["lite"] and local_file.template["full"].
each.key is the entry's key (lite) and each.value its value (m8i.xlarge). ${...} puts a value inside a string.
terraform_data is a built-in resource that only stores a value. Here it stands in for the warm pool settings: how many stopped VMs to keep ready per size.

p: When the same group of resources is needed in more than one place, you move it into a module: a folder of .tf files with variables as its inputs and outputs as its return values. You call it with a module block, much like you render a React component with props. The folder you run tofu in is itself a module, called the root module.
Modules change addresses. A resource inside a module called pool gets the address module.pool.local_file.template["lite"]. Lesson p4-3 reads and changes the real modules of our platform.

Run tofu apply on the file above and OpenTofu creates two files and the warm pool record. Run tofu plan right after that, and it says No changes. It knows this because, after every apply, it writes terraform.tfstate, a JSON file that connects each address to the real thing it created: local_file.template["full"] is the file with this ID, terraform_data.warm_pool is the record with that ID, and so on. That file is the state. Without it, OpenTofu could not tell "I must create this" apart from "I created this yesterday".

So every plan compares three things: your configuration (what should exist), the state (what OpenTofu created last time) and the real world. Before it compares, it refreshes, which means it asks the provider whether each thing in the state still exists and what it looks like now. If someone deleted sandbox-lite.txt by hand, the refresh finds it missing and the plan offers to create it again. When the real world moves away from the configuration like this, people call it drift, and a plan is how you find it.

notes.text: Change the real world without telling OpenTofu, the way a click in the AWS console would.

deeper.h: Go deeper: where state lives in a team
p: On your laptop the state is a local file. In a team it has to be shared, or each person's OpenTofu would believe it is the only one and try to create everything again. So teams keep state in a remote backend, for example an S3 bucket, with a lock that stops two applies from running at the same time.

State never goes into git. Providers save every attribute they read, and some of those are passwords or keys in plain text. The lock file .terraform.lock.hcl is a different file with a similar name: it only pins provider versions, and it does go into git.

read.h: Read the plan before you apply
p: A plan lists one block per resource that will change, with a symbol in front of it: + creates, ~ updates in place, - destroys, and -/+ destroys the old resource and then creates a replacement. The last line counts the actions, for example Plan: 1 to add, 1 to change, 1 to destroy. A replacement counts twice, once as an add and once as a destroy.

You do not choose whether a change happens in place. The provider decides it for each argument. In the plan below, the warm pool count changes in place, but the provider cannot edit the content of a file in place, so the file must be replaced, and the argument that causes it is marked # forces replacement. For a text file that does not matter. For a VM it means the machine and its disk are destroyed, and for a database it means the data is gone. That is why the habit is always the same: read the replacements and the destroys first, and only then type yes.

tofu apply prints the plan once more and waits until you type yes. In the lab you type it yourself. In our repo a person types it after the plan has been reviewed in the pull request, and an agent never does.

code.file: tofu plan after two edits to main.tf (trimmed)

notes.text: The address and the verdict, in words: this one is destroyed and created again.
-/+ is the symbol to look for first.
The reason: this argument cannot change in place.
~ means the same resource stays and only this value changes.
The replacement is the 1 to add and the 1 to destroy; the warm pool is the 1 to change.

p: State is keyed by address, so renaming a resource block looks to OpenTofu like "the old one is gone, a new one appeared". Rename local_file.template to local_file.launch_template and the plan wants to destroy two files and create two. For VMs that would be a real outage caused by a cosmetic change.

A moved block tells OpenTofu that an address changed and the thing did not: moved { from = local_file.template, to = local_file.launch_template }. The next plan says has moved to and counts 0 to add, 0 to destroy. You will use this in the lab's Fix it step.

lab.title: Plan, apply and break the sandbox sizes
needs: OpenTofu 1.10 or newer (tofu version). With Terraform, type terraform wherever the lab says tofu.
No cloud account: the lab only writes files on your laptop.
Internet for tofu init, which downloads the local provider (a few MB).
lab.goal: Describe the sandbox sizes in HCL, let OpenTofu create them, and read every kind of plan: create, no changes, drift, update in place and replace.

guess.q: OpenTofu already created the lite and full files, and the state records them. You add wide = "m8i.4xlarge" to the sizes map and run tofu plan. How many files does it plan to create?

options.text: Three: lite, full and wide, because the configuration now lists three sizes.
options.why: The state already connects lite and full to real files, and the refresh finds them, so only the difference is planned.

options.text: One: only wide, because lite and full are in the state and still exist.
options.why: The plan is the difference between what should exist and what the state and the refresh say exists. Only wide is new.

options.text: None: tofu plan fails, because the out/ folder already has files in it.
options.why: OpenTofu does not look at the folder as a whole. It checks each address in the state, and lite and full are fine.

follow.say: Make a folder for the lab and save the main.tf from the Understand step in it, because OpenTofu reads every .tf file in the folder you run it in. Then download the provider.
follow.do:
mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/p4-1 && cd ~/academy-labs/p4-1
# save main.tf here, then:
tofu init
follow.see:
- Installing hashicorp/local v2.5.3...
- Installed hashicorp/local v2.5.3 (signed, key ID 0C0AF313E5FD9F80)

OpenTofu has created a lock file .terraform.lock.hcl to record the provider
selections it made above.

OpenTofu has been successfully initialized!

follow.say: Ask for the plan, because nothing exists yet and you want to see that everything will be created before it is.
follow.see:
# local_file.template["full"] will be created
  # local_file.template["lite"] will be created
  # terraform_data.warm_pool will be created
Plan: 3 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.

follow.say: Apply it. OpenTofu shows the same plan again and waits for you, because this is the last moment to stop. Type yes.
follow.see:
Do you want to perform these actions?
  Only 'yes' will be accepted to approve.

  Enter a value: yes

terraform_data.warm_pool: Creation complete after 0s [id=c5adf14a-2d33-afb1-0555-66b14b504d3a]
local_file.template["full"]: Creation complete after 0s [id=b6bf1b60ea3f15ae2f08f0332d7d3bbc6be5c7a1]
Apply complete! Resources: 3 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.

follow.say: Plan again without changing anything, and list the state, because this is where OpenTofu's memory becomes visible.
follow.do: tofu plan | tail -1 && tofu state list
follow.see:
No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.
local_file.template["full"]
local_file.template["lite"]
terraform_data.warm_pool

follow.say: Now cause drift: delete a file by hand, the way someone might click Delete in the AWS console, and see the refresh notice it. Then let apply put it back (-auto-approve skips the yes question, so use it only in labs).
follow.do:
rm out/sandbox-lite.txt && tofu plan | grep -E '^  #|Plan:'
tofu apply -auto-approve | tail -1
follow.see:
# local_file.template["lite"] will be created
Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
Apply complete! Resources: 1 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.

follow.say: Edit main.tf: change the warm pool to full = 3. Plan, and look at the symbol, because a count can change without replacing anything.
follow.see:
# terraform_data.warm_pool will be updated in-place
          ~ full = 2 -> 3
Plan: 0 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy.

follow.say: Edit main.tf again: change full from m8i.2xlarge to m7i.2xlarge. Plan once more and find the reason for the replacement, because on a real VM this line would mean a destroyed machine.
follow.see:
# local_file.template["full"] must be replaced
-/+ resource "local_file" "template" {
      ~ content              = <<-EOT # forces replacement
  # terraform_data.warm_pool will be updated in-place
Plan: 1 to add, 1 to change, 1 to destroy.

follow.say: Undo both edits in main.tf (full is m8i.2xlarge and the warm pool is 2 again) and check that the plan is empty, so you start the Build step from a clean place.
follow.see: No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.

lab.build: Add the wide size: wide = "m8i.4xlarge" in the sizes map, and wide = 0 in the warm pool, because wide machines are rare and are not kept warm. Before you run anything, write down what you expect the plan's last line to say. Then run tofu plan, compare it with your guess, apply it, and run tofu plan once more.
checks: Your plan says Plan: 1 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy (the wide file is added, the warm pool record changes in place).
ls out shows sandbox-full.txt, sandbox-lite.txt and sandbox-wide.txt, and sandbox-wide.txt says instance_type = m8i.4xlarge.
tofu state list shows four addresses, including local_file.template["wide"].
A second tofu plan right after the apply says No changes.
You did not edit or delete terraform.tfstate by hand at any point.
lab.fix: A teammate tidies the code and renames the resource from "template" to "launch_template", because that is what it really is. They open a PR with the line "just a rename, no changes". Make the same rename and run tofu plan: it wants to destroy all your files and create them again (Plan: 3 to add, 0 to change, 3 to destroy). On real launch templates in use, that is not "no changes". Fix it without undoing the rename: add a moved block from local_file.template to local_file.launch_template, plan again, and reach 0 to add and 0 to destroy. When you finish, run tofu destroy and type yes, so the lab leaves nothing behind.
explain: After the first apply, why did the second tofu plan say No changes instead of planning the files again?
You deleted a file by hand and the plan wanted to create it again. Which three things did OpenTofu compare to decide that?
Changing the warm pool count was ~ but changing the machine type was -/+. Who decides which one you get, and why should you read -/+ lines first?
lab.done: You added wide with a plan of 1 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy, the next plan said No changes, and tofu destroy at the end removed all four resources.

check.q: After an apply, a teammate deletes terraform.tfstate by accident. The files in out/ are still there. What does the next tofu plan say?

options.text: No changes, because the files already exist.
options.why: OpenTofu does not search the disk or the cloud for things that look right. Without the state, it has no record that these files are its own.

options.text: It plans to create every resource again, because nothing records that the existing files belong to this configuration.
options.why: The state is the only link between an address and a real thing. On AWS this would try to create duplicate machines, or fail on names that are already taken.

options.text: It reads the out/ folder and writes a new state from it.
options.why: The refresh only checks things that are already in the state. Adopting an existing thing is a separate, deliberate step called import.

check.q: A plan shows -/+ next to an aws_instance, with # forces replacement on the image ID. What will apply do?

options.text: Update the running VM in place with the new image.
options.why: In place is ~. The provider says the image of an existing VM cannot change, so it marks a replacement.

options.text: Only update the state, because the VM is already running.
options.why: Apply changes real resources first, and then records the result in the state.

options.text: Destroy the VM together with its disk, and then create a new one.
options.why: That is what -/+ means. Read the reason line and decide whether losing that machine is what you want before you type yes.

check.q: Nobody changed main.tf, but today tofu plan says 1 to add. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: Something changed outside OpenTofu, for example a file or a VM was deleted by hand, and the refresh noticed it.
options.why: This is drift. The plan compares the configuration with the state and with the real world, so a change made by hand appears as work to do.

options.text: OpenTofu creates every resource again on each plan, to be safe.
options.why: A plan only lists differences. Right after an apply, the plan says No changes.
Then the plan would want to create every resource, not one. One missing thing points to that one thing changing.

p: Our infrastructure repo, RhinoHealth/infrastructure, runs OpenTofu 1.12.6 together with Terragrunt, which the next lesson explains. The sandbox sizes are a real for_each over { lite = "m8i.xlarge", full = "m8i.2xlarge", wide = "m8i.4xlarge" } in modules/aws-sandbox-pool. There the resource is an aws_launch_template instead of a file, and the warm pool sizes (lite 2, full 2, wide 0 to start) are a second map that the Auto Scaling groups read.

State lives in the S3 bucket rhinohealth-terraform-state with a lock file, one state file per folder. Plans are run on a laptop over VPN and pasted into the PR, and a person from DevOps applies after review. Agents may write HCL and run checks, but they never apply; p4-6 shows how that is enforced.

tickets.why: One launch template per size with for_each over the sizes map: the shape of this lab, with aws_launch_template.
Warm pools per size (lite 2, full 2, wide 0), read from a second map, like the warm_pool record here.
The ai-agents account's Terragrunt tree: plan locally, paste it into the PR, a person applies.

words.plain: The open-source fork of Terraform that our infrastructure repo runs. Same HCL, same commands, the program is called tofu.
A plugin that talks to one system (aws, local, vault) and manages its resources.
One thing a provider manages, written as resource "<type>" "<name>"; its address is <type>.<name>.
The file where OpenTofu records which real thing belongs to which address. Shared and locked in a team, never in git.
The list of actions OpenTofu would take to make the real world match the configuration: + create, ~ update, -/+ replace, - destroy.
When the real world no longer matches the configuration because someone changed it by hand. A plan shows it.

review.q: Explain to a teammate, without the word "diff", what tofu plan compares, and why it needs the state for that.
review.a: It compares the configuration (what should exist), the state (what it created last time) and the real world (through a refresh). Without the state it cannot connect an address to a real thing, so it would plan to create everything again.

review.q: You see Plan: 2 to add, 0 to change, 2 to destroy for a change that was "only a rename". What happened, and what do you do?
review.a: Renaming a resource changes its address, so OpenTofu thinks the old one is gone and a new one is needed. Add a moved block from the old address to the new one; the plan should then show 0 to add and 0 to destroy.

review.q: Which of these go into git: main.tf, .terraform.lock.hcl, terraform.tfstate, .terraform/?
review.a: main.tf and .terraform.lock.hcl. The state can hold secrets and belongs in a locked remote backend, and .terraform/ is the downloaded providers, like node_modules.

remember: Write what should exist, let the plan show the difference from the state and the real world, and read every replace and destroy before you type yes.
